Potassium: low and high, mild / moderate / severe

Hospitalist Toolkit · Electrolytes tab · adults · SI units · normal K 3.5–5.0 mmol/L · always check Mg, creatinine and an ECG when K is abnormal
Decision-support draft, not verified. Written by Claude; doses are typical adult doses. Check against Island Health protocols and pharmacy. Guideline = stated in a guideline; Practice = common practice (no guideline sets this).

Low potassium (hypokalemia)

MildModerateSevere
K (mmol/L)3.0–3.42.5–2.9< 2.5, or any level with ECG changes, weakness or arrhythmia
Symptoms / ECGUsually noneWeakness, cramps, constipation; flat T, U wavesParalysis, ileus, rhabdomyolysis; ST depression, long QU, ectopy, VT/VF, torsades (worse with digoxin, ischemia, low Mg)

PotassiumK-Dur 20 mEq SR 1–2 tabs PO BID (40–80 mEq/day)K-Dur 20 mEq × 2 PO BID–TID; or KCl 10 mEq/100 mL IV peripheral bags, each ≥ 30 min Local sheetPeripheral: KCl 10 mEq/100 mL bags, each ≥ 30 min. Central only: KCl 20 mEq/50 mL or 40 mEq/100 mL (rate per IV manual) Local sheet. Plus PO if able; not in dextrose
MagnesiumCheck; PO or MgSO4 2 g IV if lowMgSO4 2 g IV, or 5 g if Mg < 0.6 Local sheetMgSO4 5 g IV, max 2 g/h (2 g over 10–15 min first if torsades)

Causes of low K

  • Kidney loss: loop/thiazide diuretics, osmotic diuresis, metabolic alkalosis, aldosterone excess (hypertension), low Mg, amphotericin, RTA, Gitelman/Bartter
  • GI loss: vomiting / NG suction, diarrhea, laxatives, high-output stoma
  • Shift into cells: insulin (DKA), salbutamol, refeeding, alkalosis, periodic paralysis
  • Spot urine K:Cr > 1.5 mmol/mmol = kidney loss; < 1.5 = GI, shift or intake

Good to know

  • 100–200 mEq raises K by about 1 mmol/L in acute loss; up to 400 mEq in chronic loss Local sheet
  • How long: K 3.0 → 4.0 needs about 100–200 mEq (acute) to 400 mEq (chronic); at 80–120 mEq/day PO that is about 1–3 days (acute) or 2–5 days (chronic) Practice. Keep a maintenance dose while diuretic or GI losses continue
  • Products: KCl 8 mEq SR (Slow-K), 20 mEq SR (K-Dur), elixir 1.33 mEq/mL (salty, dilute), K citrate 25 mEq (~40% as effective); premixed KCl 20 or 40 mEq/L in 1 L Local sheet
  • Target ≥ 4.0 with AF, ischemia, heart failure or digoxin
  • DKA: hold insulin until K ≥ 3.3
  • GFR < 30: 50% dose, monitor more often Local sheet
  • Ongoing diuretic loss: add spironolactone or amiloride rather than more KCl
  • K that will not correct = replace Mg

High potassium (hyperkalemia)

MildModerateSevere
K (mmol/L)5.1–5.9 UKKA: mild 5.5–5.96.0–6.4 UKKA≥ 6.5 UKKA, or any level with ECG changes
FirstIs it real? Hemolysis, high platelets (> 500) or WBC (> 50): repeat as plasma K12-lead ECG urgently (all K ≥ 6.0) UKKAContinuous cardiac monitor UKKA; 12-lead ECG now
Protect heart–Only if ECG changesECG changes: calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL (3 g) IV over 5–10 min; repeat if ECG still abnormal after 5 min
Shift–Insulin regular 10 units IV + dextrose 25 g (5 units if eGFR < 30); salbutamol 10–20 mg nebSame; sodium bicarbonate only with metabolic acidosis
RemoveStop K-raising drugs, low-K diet, SZC (Lokelma) 10 g daily or patiromer 8.4 g dailySZC 10 g TID up to 48 h; furosemide if not dry; IV fluid if drySame; dialysis if refractory, oliguric AKI or ESRD (nephrology early)
Repeat labsK within 24 h (24–72 h if stable, cause clear); 6–12 h if AKI PracticeK at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 h after treatment UKKAK at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 h UKKA; aim K < 6.0 at 2 h
Glucose–At 0, 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, 300, 360 min after insulin-glucose (at least 6 h) UKKASame UKKA

Causes of high K

  • False high: hemolysis, tourniquet / fist clenching, very high platelets or WBC
  • Low excretion: AKI, CKD, low aldosterone (diabetes / type 4 RTA, adrenal insufficiency, heparin), obstruction
  • Drugs: ACEi, ARB, ARNI, spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone, amiloride, trimethoprim, NSAIDs, heparin/LMWH, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, beta-blockers, digoxin toxicity, K supplements
  • Shift out: insulin deficiency, acidosis, hyperosmolality
  • Cell breakdown: rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, hemolysis, GI bleed

Good to know

  • Calcium protects the heart for 30–60 min only: it does not lower K
  • Insulin effect wears off at 4–6 h: rebound K is why the 4 and 6 h checks matter
  • Hypoglycemia after insulin-glucose is common with low eGFR
  • Digoxin toxicity with high K: digoxin immune Fab
  • Restart RAAS blockers later at a lower dose with a binder when they matter (HF, CKD)
